title: Quantization technical review - Hydra Systems
summary: Redwood SE + AE walk Hydra Systems through INT8/FP8/GPTQ/AWQ tradeoffs, observed accuracy regressions, and recommended runtime/batching/KV cache settings for on-prem VPC deployment. Customer requests benchmarks on their 4k-token RAG workload and asks about QAT vs PTQ and fallback policies.
topics: KV cache and prefix caching impacts
batching strategies for low-latency vs throughput
transcript:
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Samir Patel from Redwood, AE on this account. We also have Lena, our inference SE. How are you all?
[00:08] Mark: Good, thanks. Mark here. We have Priya and Alex also on.
[00:12] Priya: Hi. Thanks for scheduling, excited to dig in.
[00:15] Lena: Great, quick agenda: we'll run through quantization options (INT8, FP8, GPTQ, AWQ), show some perf numbers, talk KV cache and batching, and then discuss on-prem/VPC caveats. We'll leave 15 mins for Q&A.
[00:28] Alex: Sounds good. We're particularly worried about regressions on our RAG pipelines for 4k token contexts.
[00:33] Lena: Totally. We prepared a few benchmark cases that mimic RAG with 3-4k context lengths and mixed decode/generation.
[00:40] Samir: Quick qualification - what's your infra? Alex?
[00:43] Alex: We're on-prem right now. NVIDIA H100s, DGX-ish clusters, private VPC, strict egress rules. We plan to pilot Redwood Private in our DC.
[00:51] Priya: And models: we run Llama-2-13B variants and a custom finetuned 70B for some research. The 13B is more production.
[00:59] Lena: Ok good, that helps. So to start, high-level on quantization: INT8 gives big perf/cost wins with small to moderate accuracy hits depending on model and task; FP8 can preserve more fidelity but requires hardware support and more engineering. GPTQ/AWQ are PTQ variants that target minimal accuracy loss with different algorithmic tradeoffs.
[01:18] Mark: Can you unpack AWQ vs GPTQ a bit? We've seen both in GitHub repos but not sure which to use.
[01:25] Lena: Sure. GPTQ is older, does layer-wise quantization often with per-channel scales and some second-order info; AWQ is newer, tends to yield better accuracy at 4-bit/INT8 ranges for many LLMs by optimizing weight approximations and per-group scaling. In our internal benchmarks AWQ often gives slightly better NLI/QA scores than naive GPTQ at same bitwidth.
[01:41] Priya: Any cases where GPTQ is preferable?
[01:44] Lena: GPTQ has broader community tool support for more model families. AWQ can be more sensitive to quantize-time hyperparams. So if you need reproducible, well-documented pipelines, GPTQ might be safer, but AWQ often wins on raw accuracy.
[01:58] Alex: What about INT8 vs FP8? Our cards support FP8 via Ampere or H100 float8 kernels?
[02:05] Lena: H100 supports some FP8 paths, yes. FP8 can get you closer to FP16 accuracy, but kernel maturity and runtime support vary. INT8 is very mature and gives large throughput gains especially with optimized kernels. If you have H100 and need highest accuracy, FP8 is worth experimenting with; but INT8 AWQ is usually cost-advantageous.
[02:24] Samir: Quick note on Redwood runtime: we do automatic kernel selection - the runtime selects the best kernel path based on model architecture, seq length distribution, and hardware. So for H100 we pick FP8 kernels if available and if the model/profile indicates better latency/accuracy tradeoff.
[02:40] Mark: Nice. Can the runtime fallback automatically if a quantized variant has a regression?
[02:45] Lena: Yes - we support policy-based fallbacks. You can configure an automatic rollback to a higher-precision variant (FP16 or FP32) if eval metrics cross a threshold. We tie regressions to prompt sets so we can detect task-specific drop-offs.
[02:58] Priya: That rollback seems critical. How fast is eviction or switch? We need sub-minute reaction during pilot.
[03:04] Lena: Switch is near-instant for new requests; in-flight requests finish on the existing backend but new connections route to the fallback. Usually within 30-90s for routing to converge depending on autoscaler and capacity.
[03:16] Alex: Good. Let's look at perf numbers you mentioned.
[03:20] Lena: Right, slide I'm referencing - for Llama-2-13B on H100 with 2k context, INT8 AWQ delivered ~2.8x throughput vs FP16 with 6-8% latency decrease at median token times, while end-task accuracy (QA exact match) degraded 0.8-1.5%, depending on prompt formatting. FP8 ran about 1.6x vs FP16 with <0.5% accuracy loss on average.
[03:41] Mark: Ok those are helpful. But our RAG patterns hit 4k often; how does KV cache factor in?
[03:47] Lena: Good question. KV cache size grows linearly with sequence length; bigger contexts mean more memory and slower KV lookups if not optimized. Our runtime uses compressed KV caching and selective prefix caching: for RAG we can cache document embeddings and the initial prompt prefix so decode only needs to attend to the retrieval chunk plus user input.
[04:06] Priya: Are those compressions lossy? Any accuracy hit?
[04:09] Lena: Most of our KV compression is lossless or near-lossless - it's more encoding and layout optimization. The tradeoff is CPU overhead on compression/uncompression, but that is usually worth it for memory savings at long contexts.
[04:20] Samir: Also note batching interacts with KV cache: larger batches increase throughput but you have to rehydrate KV cache per instance unless you use shared prefix caching. We have a few strategies: per-request KV, shared prefix caching, and microbatching to balance latency.
[04:35] Alex: Can you explain microbatching?
[04:37] Lena: Microbatching breaks a big batch into small microbatches that feed through the GPU sequentially, reducing tail latencies. It keeps utilization high but avoids large latency spikes for single requests. Good for conversational workloads.
[04:48] Priya: For our SLA we need 95th percentile token latency < 120ms for 1-2 token turns. Any recommendations?
[04:55] Lena: For that, go with dedicated instances on H100, INT8 AWQ for 13B, small batching (2-4) and aggressive prefix caching. Also set a latency-based routing policy to prefer local region and dedicated capacity.
[05:06] Mark: How about model accuracy regressions - what's your eval pipeline?
[05:09] Lena: We run prompt-set based evals. For each model/quantized variant we track a set of canonical prompts across NLI, QA, summarization, and your domain-specific RAG examples. We record EM/F1, BLEU, and hallucination heuristics. If any metric drops beyond configured thresholds, we flag and either pause rollout or roll back.
[05:25] Priya: Can we upload our RAG prompt set?
[05:27] Samir: Absolutely - we'll provide a secure upload link. We also recommend adding synthetic edge-case prompts that expose truncation or tokenization issues.
[05:36] Alex: On the on-prem side - how does Redwood Private integrate with our KMS and HSM?
[05:41] Lena: Private supports KMS integrations and HSM-backed key wrapping. Your infra team will run the control plane in a private subnet; logs are forwarded to your SIEM. We support SAML SSO and RBAC for tenant isolation.
[05:52] Alex: Any special network egress for quantization? We prefer zero outbound.
[05:56] Samir: For Private you can opt for fully air-gapped; some features like automated model onboarding or benchmark telemetry require outbound but can be disabled. We'll provide offline model packages and local benchmarking tooling.
[06:08] Priya: Awesome. Back to quantization: what's the recommended workflow? PTQ with AWQ first, then QAT if needed?
[06:15] Lena: Yes - start with PTQ (AWQ/GPTQ) as it's fast and often sufficient. If you see targeted regressions in safety or hallucination-prone prompts, then QAT (quant-aware fine-tuning) on a small dataset can recover accuracy at cost of more compute and data. QAT also reduces brittleness for certain operators.
[06:31] Mark: How much time does QAT usually take for a 13B?
[06:34] Lena: For a small QAT run (few epochs on a focused dataset) it's on the order of several hours on a couple of H100s. Full retrain is longer.
[06:42] Priya: Are there tooling integrations for QAT?
[06:44] Lena: We integrate with customers' training infra or can run QAT as a Redwood-managed job in Private. We also provide a Jupyter-based notebook and a reproducible job spec.
[06:54] Alex: We keep seeing occasional tokenization mismatches when switching quantized variants. Is that a runtime issue?
[06:58] Lena: Tokenization should be identical; mismatches usually stem from subtle prompt formatting or whitespace handling. We recommend canonicalizing inputs pre-tokenization and adding a few sanity tests in the eval set.
[07:10] Samir: Quick demo - Lena, can you run the 13B AWQ infer on a RAG example?
[07:14] Lena: Sure, initiating the demo - running a retrieval plus generation on a 3.8k context.
[07:22] [07:22] Lena: (typing) -- runtime logs show KV rehyration, batch size 2, microbatch 1. Latency per token ~95ms median, 140ms 95th. Output EM dropped 1.2% vs FP16 on our sample prompt set.
[07:40] Priya: Those 95th percentiles are close to our threshold. If we tune microbatching and prefix caching is it likely to drop below 120ms?
[07:47] Lena: Yes, with prefix caching and smaller decode batch you should be able to shave 15-25% off the 95th. Also pin to dedicated capacity rather than shared.
[07:57] Mark: Any memory concerns for 70B finetuned model if we quantize to INT8?
[08:02] Lena: 70B INT8 reduces memory substantially but still large - you will likely need model partitioning and multi-GPU sharding. Our runtime supports sequence parallelism and tensor parallel. For 70B we often recommend a combination of FP8 where needed and INT8 for less sensitive layers.
[08:18] Priya: How do you measure which layers are "sensitive"?
[08:21] Lena: We analyze per-layer activation distributions and run a layer-sensitivity sweep - essentially quantize one layer at a time and measure downstream metric impact. We automate this and produce a sensitivity map to guide mixed-precision configs.
[08:34] Alex: That sounds useful. Will you share the layer sensitivity report for our finetuned 70B if we provide model artifacts?
[08:39] Samir: Yes, as part of the pilot we'll run the sensitivity analysis and share a report in the secure workspace.
[08:48] Mark: A question on latency vs cost - are your pricing models per-token unchanged for quantized models? Or do we get discounts for dedicated commits?
[08:55] Samir: For Hosted public API we bill based on token math but quantized models that improve throughput can lower effective per-token cost. For Dedicated and Private we provide reserved capacity pricing; we'd model the unit economics for your expected QPS and token mix and show the delta between FP16 and INT8 run costs. We'll send a cost model.
[09:10] Priya: Great. For our acceptance criteria: maintain >=98% of baseline F1 on our RAG eval and 95th percentile latency <120ms. Are those achievable?
[09:19] Lena: Achievable with dedicated H100s, INT8 AWQ for 13B, prefix caching, and tuned batching. We'll need your eval set to validate.
[09:27] Alex: What's the best way to run our RAG benchmarks against Redwood Private?
[09:30] Lena: We'll provide a benchmarking harness - a Docker image you can run in your cluster that hits the local Redwood Private endpoints and uploads result artifacts to a secure bucket (or keeps them local if you want). It measures token latencies, throughput, and task metrics.
[09:42] Mark: Good. About regression alerts - can we get Slack/webhook notifications?
[09:46] Samir: Yes, we integrate with Slack, PagerDuty, and custom webhooks for alerts. You can configure thresholds per-metric.
[09:53] Priya: Any gotchas we should watch for when converting our finetuned weights?
[09:58] Lena: Watch custom operators, fused kernels, and any nonstandard attention modifications. Also ensure any tokenizers or special embeddings are preserved. For finetuned adapters, sometimes it's safer to quantize the base and keep adapters in higher precision.
[10:13] Mark: Are there documented cases where AWQ produced hallucination increases?
[10:17] Lena: Rare, but yes - sometimes quantization can shift logits in ways that increase spurious generation in open-ended prompts. That's why we recommend targeted eval sets and automatic rollback policies.
[10:27] Alex: Ok let's cover next steps and action items.
[10:30] Samir: I'll recap.
[10:31] Samir: Next steps: 1) We'll send the secure upload link for your RAG eval prompt set. 2) Redwood runs sensitivity analysis on your 13B (and optionally 70B) artifacts. 3) We'll share a cost model comparing FP16 vs INT8 for your expected traffic. 4) We'll provide the benchmarking harness for on-prem runs.
[10:50] Priya: Timeline?
[10:52] Samir: We can deliver the initial sensitivity report and benchmark config in about 5 business days after we get artifacts. Cost model the same day.
[10:59] Mark: Great. Any blockers for us?
[11:02] Lena: Only that we need the model files or a way to reproduce your finetune. If you prefer we can run on a sanitized public replica first.
[11:11] Alex: We'll get you the 13B weights and a sanitized prompt set.
[11:15] Priya: Also please include recommended config for microbatching and prefix cache settings.
[11:18] Samir: Will do.
[11:20] Mark: Anything else?
[11:22] Samir: That's it. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the links and schedule the next checkpoint.
[11:28] Priya: Thanks.
[11:29] Lena: Thanks all.
